overview: Two types of connective tissue in the skeletal system, differing mainly in rigidity, blood supply, and mineral content.
genZNote: Cartilage: flexible and rubbery. Bone: rigid and mineralised.

aspects.label: Rigidity
aspects.valueA: Flexible and somewhat elastic, due to a matrix rich in collagen and chondroitin.
aspects.valueB: Rigid and hard, due to a matrix impregnated with calcium salts.

aspects.label: Blood Supply
aspects.valueA: Avascular — lacks its own direct blood supply, so it heals slowly.
aspects.valueB: Highly vascular — has a rich blood supply, allowing it to heal more readily.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Ear pinna, tip of the nose, intervertebral discs.

aspects.label: Developmental Relationship
aspects.valueA: Often serves as the initial template that is later replaced by bone during development (ossification).
aspects.valueB: Forms through ossification, often replacing an earlier cartilage model.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Most of the human skeleton starts out as cartilage in the embryo and is gradually replaced by bone through a process called ossification.
overlay.memoryTrick: Cartilage = flexible, no blood supply, heals slowly. Bone = rigid, rich blood supply, heals faster.
overlay.commonMisconception: Not all cartilage gets replaced by bone — some, like the cartilage in your ears and nose tip, remains cartilage throughout life.
